group.title: Philosophy and ideas
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is and how we can know things.
examples: Her thesis in {epistemology} asks how we can trust our senses.
wrong: Epistemology is the study of how plants grow in different soils.

words.meaning: The branch of philosophy that asks what exists and what it means for something to be.
examples: In {ontology}, philosophers debate whether numbers really exist.
wrong: Ontology is the art of cooking meals for large groups.

words.meaning: The part of philosophy that deals with the basic nature of reality, time, mind and being.
examples: Questions about whether time truly passes belong to {metaphysics}.
wrong: Metaphysics is a practical course on fixing car engines.

words.meaning: The view that knowledge comes mainly from experience and what we observe.
examples: Modern science grew out of a spirit of {empiricism}.
wrong: His empiricism made him refuse to look at any evidence at all.

words.meaning: The view that reason, not the senses, is the main source of knowledge.
examples: Her {rationalism} led her to trust logic over first impressions.
wrong: His rationalism meant he made every choice by pure feeling and impulse.

words.meaning: The belief that life has no meaning and that values have no real basis.
examples: The novel’s hero drifts into {nihilism} after losing everything he believed in.
wrong: Her nihilism gave her a deep sense that every moment of life was full of purpose.

words.meaning: The idea that only your own mind is sure to exist; also, being totally absorbed in yourself.
examples: The film’s narrator sinks into a kind of {solipsism}, unable to imagine other people’s thoughts.
wrong: His solipsism made him think constantly about the feelings of others.

words.meaning: The belief that every event, including human choice, is fully caused by what happened before.
examples: If {determinism} is true, can anyone be blamed for their actions?
wrong: Determinism is the belief that events happen with no cause at all.

words.meaning: The view that the right action is the one that brings the greatest good to the most people.
examples: Under {utilitarianism}, the policy that helps the most people is the moral one.
wrong: Utilitarianism says we should ignore how our actions affect other people.

words.meaning: A philosophy that says people create their own meaning through free choice and responsibility.
examples: The play is a classic of {existentialism}: its characters must invent a reason to live.
wrong: Existentialism teaches that our purpose is fixed for us before we are born.

words.meaning: A way of finding truth by setting opposing ideas against each other and resolving them.
examples: The seminar moved forward through a {dialectic} of claim and counterclaim.
wrong: Their dialectic was a quiet agreement in which nobody raised a different view.

words.meaning: A form of reasoning where a conclusion follows from two linked statements.
examples: All birds have feathers; a robin is a bird; so a robin has feathers: a classic {syllogism}.
wrong: A syllogism is a random guess with no reasoning behind it.

words.meaning: A statement that says the same thing twice in different words, or is true by definition.
examples: "A free gift" is a {tautology}, since all gifts are free.
wrong: "It may rain tomorrow" is a tautology because it adds new information.

words.meaning: Known by reasoning alone, before or without experience.
examples: That a triangle has three sides is {a priori} knowledge.
wrong: We gained this a priori knowledge only by running many experiments.

words.meaning: Known only through experience or evidence, not by reasoning alone.
examples: Whether water boils at a lower point on mountains is {a posteriori}: you have to test it.
wrong: This a posteriori truth can be known without any observation at all.

words.meaning: The study or explanation of things in terms of their purpose or goal.
examples: Older biology relied on {teleology}, saying eyes exist in order to see.
wrong: Teleology explains things only by their cause, never by their purpose.

words.meaning: Calmly accepting pain or difficulty without complaining; also an ancient school of thought teaching this.
examples: She faced the long illness with remarkable {stoicism}.
wrong: His stoicism showed when he screamed and complained about every small problem.

words.meaning: The belief that pleasure is the most important goal in life.
examples: The resort sells pure {hedonism}: food, sun and no responsibilities.
wrong: Her hedonism made her give up every pleasure to live like a monk.

words.meaning: The view that truth and right and wrong depend on culture or person, not on fixed standards.
examples: Moral {relativism} holds that no culture’s values are better than another’s.
wrong: Relativism insists that one universal standard of truth applies to everyone.

words.meaning: An attitude of doubting claims until there is good proof.
examples: The report was met with {skepticism} by other scientists.
wrong: Her skepticism made her believe every rumor she heard.

words.meaning: Stating opinions as if they were certainly true, without accepting any doubt or debate.
examples: The debate went nowhere because of the speaker’s {dogmatism}.
wrong: His dogmatism made him happy to change his mind whenever someone disagreed.

words.meaning: Going beyond ordinary experience or the physical world.
examples: Many describe the music as a {transcendent} experience.
wrong: The film was so transcendent that it felt dull, ordinary and forgettable.

words.meaning: Existing or present within something, especially within the world rather than beyond it.
examples: Some thinkers see the divine as {immanent} in nature itself.
wrong: If a quality is immanent in a thing, it exists only far outside it.

words.meaning: Able to feel and be aware of things.
examples: The law protects animals as {sentient} beings.
wrong: A rock is a sentient object that feels everything around it.

words.meaning: Disproving a claim by showing that it leads to a ridiculous conclusion.
examples: Her {reductio ad absurdum} showed the rule would ban breathing.
wrong: His reductio ad absurdum proved the idea by showing how sensible its results were.

words.meaning: To think carefully and seriously about something.
examples: The committee {cogitated} for weeks before deciding.
wrong: He cogitated on the offer without giving it a single thought.

words.meaning: A general idea not based on any real, particular thing.
examples: Justice is an {abstraction}, but its effects are very real.
wrong: A chair in your kitchen is a perfect example of an abstraction.

words.meaning: The view that reality has two basic parts, such as mind and matter.
examples: His {dualism} treats the mind as separate from the body.
wrong: Dualism claims that reality is made of one single substance.

words.meaning: The philosophical view that only physical matter truly exists.
examples: In {materialism}, thoughts are just activity in the brain.
wrong: Materialism says that physical matter does not exist at all.

words.meaning: The philosophical view that reality is built from minds and ideas.
examples: Her {idealism} claims objects exist only as ideas in a mind.
wrong: Idealism holds that ideas play no part in what is real.

words.meaning: The most basic truths from which other ideas are built.
examples: Let’s reason from {first principles} instead of copying old answers.
wrong: Working from first principles means copying what everyone else already does.

words.meaning: To argue in a circle, assuming the very thing you are trying to prove.
examples: Saying the book is true because it says so is to {beg the question}.
wrong: Her argument begged the question, because it relied only on independent evidence.

words.meaning: An imagined situation used to test an idea through reasoning.
examples: The famous {thought experiment} asks whether a ship with every part replaced is the same ship.
wrong: A thought experiment needs a laboratory full of real chemicals.

words.meaning: The basic experience of being human, including birth, love, struggle and death.
examples: Great novels explore {the human condition}.
wrong: The human condition is a disease that only doctors can catch.

words.meaning: The power to make your own choices, not controlled by fate or outside forces.
examples: Do we have {free will}, or are our choices already decided?
wrong: Because he acted out of free will, someone else had forced him to do it.

words.meaning: So clear that it needs no proof or explanation.
examples: To her, the need for change was {self-evident}.
wrong: The answer was self-evident, so nobody could understand it without a long proof.

words.meaning: A statement so obviously true that it is hardly worth saying.
examples: "Time will tell" is a {truism}, not an answer.
wrong: His truism was a shocking new idea nobody had ever heard.

words.meaning: Not committed to believing or denying something because it cannot be known.
examples: I’m {agnostic} about which design is better until we see the data.
wrong: She’s agnostic on the issue, so she argues for one side with total certainty.

words.meaning: Accepted as true without needing proof.
examples: It is {axiomatic} that a good teacher must listen.
wrong: The claim was axiomatic, so everyone demanded proof before accepting it.

words.meaning: Clever but misleading reasoning, especially about right and wrong.
examples: His excuse for keeping the money was pure {casuistry}.
wrong: Her casuistry was a simple, honest argument anyone could follow.
